Responder Analysis: Who Cleared the Threshold, by Group

Source: R/responder_analysis.R
responder_analysis.Rd

Reports the proportion of each group whose outcome reaches a meaningful threshold (a minimal clinically important difference, a remission cut, a mastery criterion), a clinical and behavioral endpoint that a mean difference does not show. For each group the function reports the responder count and proportion with a Wilson confidence interval; with exactly two groups it adds the risk difference with the Newcombe (1998) score-based hybrid interval and the number needed to treat with its confidence set; and across any number of groups it reports the omnibus chi square test of equal responder proportions. An optional sweep repeats the analysis over a grid of thresholds, making explicit how conclusions depend on where the line is drawn, disclosing the threshold dependence that any single-threshold claim leaves implicit.

Usage

responder_analysis(
  x,
  group,
  threshold,
  direction = c("ge", "le"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  sweep = NULL
)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of outcomes (for example, change scores).

group

Group labels, one per observation (coerced to factor; the first level is the reference for the two-group difference). An observation with a missing outcome or a missing label is removed, and a level left with no observation is dropped.

threshold

The cut defining response: a single number, fixed before the data are seen (see Assumptions).

direction

"ge" (default): a responder has x >= threshold; "le": x <= threshold (for outcomes where lower is better). An outcome exactly at the threshold is a responder under either direction.

conf_level

Confidence level for all intervals. Defaults to 0.95.

sweep

Optional numeric vector of additional thresholds; the analysis is repeated at each and stacked with a leading threshold column. threshold comes first, then the values of sweep in the order given, each distinct value once.

Value

A tidy wide data.frame (class dmar_responder, a dmar_tbl) with columns group, n, responders, estimate, ci_lower, ci_upper, chi_square, df, and p_value, and these rows:

  • One row per group, named by its level: the group size n, the number of responders, the responder proportion in estimate, and its Wilson limits. The three test columns are NA.

  • difference (two groups only): the second proportion minus the first in estimate, with the Newcombe limits. n, responders, and the test columns are NA.

  • nnt (two groups only): \(1/|d|\) in estimate (Inf when the difference is 0), with its limits when the interval for the difference excludes zero and NA limits otherwise. The other columns are NA.

  • omnibus: chi_square, df, and p_value of the test of equal proportions. The other columns are NA.

When sweep is supplied, the same table is stacked per threshold with a leading threshold column.

With two groups the result carries two attributes. nnt_set is "interval" or "two_intervals", one value per threshold. nnt_confidence_set is a data.frame with columns lower and upper (preceded by threshold under sweep) and one row per interval of the set, on the signed scale \(1/\Delta\): one row, (1 / ci_upper, 1 / ci_lower) of the difference row, for "interval"; and for "two_intervals" the rows (-Inf, 1 / ci_lower) and (1 / ci_upper, Inf). For two intervals a line printed under the table states the set, and names each side by the group that responds more often there, from the group_labels attribute (the two levels of group, in order). The attributes belong to the table itself: tidy() and glance() return the rows without them, and a table made by rbind() or by taking rows keeps the attributes of the first table, as every dmar_tbl does. The confidence level is in the conf_level attribute.

Details

What is estimated. For each group, the proportion of its population whose outcome is at or beyond the threshold, \(\pi_g\). With two groups, the difference of the two proportions, \(\Delta = \pi_2 - \pi_1\) (second level of group minus the first), and the number needed to treat, \(1/|\Delta|\): the number of people who would have to be moved from the first condition to the second for one more of them, on average, to be a responder. This is the number needed to treat of evidence based medicine, a function of two response proportions at a stated threshold. It is not the quantity nnt_from_smd returns, which is computed from a standardized mean difference under a normal model, involves no threshold, and is smaller for a positive effect (see Which NNT this is on that page).

Assumptions. The observations are independent, and with two groups the groups are independent of each other (two arms of a randomized trial, not two occasions for the same people; for paired proportions see ci_proportion_paired). The threshold is fixed in advance. Every interval and the test condition on the threshold as a known constant, so a threshold chosen after the data are seen, for instance the one at which the difference is largest, makes the stated confidence level and the p-value wrong, and no adjustment is made for it here. sweep describes how the result depends on the threshold; it is not a search, and the rows of a sweep are not adjusted for one another.

The interval for each proportion. With \(r\) responders among \(n\), \(p = r/n\), and \(z\) the \(1 - \alpha/2\) quantile of the standard normal distribution, the Wilson score limits are $$\frac{p + z^2/(2n) \mp z \sqrt{p(1 - p)/n + z^2/(4n^2)}}{1 + z^2/n},$$ the same limits ci_proportion returns. They lie inside [0, 1] for every count, the counts 0 and \(n\) included, where the limit at the boundary is exactly 0 or 1 (and can be computed as a number within about \(10^{-16}\) of it).

The interval for the difference. The two-group risk difference uses Newcombe's method 10: the difference interval is assembled from the two Wilson limits, which keeps it inside [-1, 1] and well behaved at boundary counts. With \((l_1, u_1)\) and \((l_2, u_2)\) the Wilson limits of the first and second group and \(d = p_2 - p_1\), the limits computed are $$d - \sqrt{(p_2 - l_2)^2 + (u_1 - p_1)^2} \quad \mbox{and} \quad d + \sqrt{(u_2 - p_2)^2 + (p_1 - l_1)^2}.$$

The number needed to treat and its confidence set. The nnt row holds \(1/|d|\), an absolute value; the direction is the sign of the difference row. Its limits come from the limits of the difference, and what they are depends on where zero falls:

  • Zero outside the interval for the difference: the reciprocals of the two limits, in absolute value, are the limits of the number needed to treat, the smaller in ci_lower and the larger in ci_upper.

  • Zero inside the interval: a difference of zero is a number needed to treat of infinity, so the confidence set is every value at least as large as the reciprocal of one limit in one direction, together with every value at least as large as the reciprocal of the other limit in the other direction. These are two intervals that meet at infinity (Altman, 1998), which one lower and one upper limit cannot hold, so the two limits of the nnt row are NA.

In both cases the set is recorded in the nnt_confidence_set attribute on the signed scale \(1/\Delta\), where a negative value means that the first group responds more often, and when it is two intervals a line under the table states it, as nnt_from_smd does. The set has the coverage of the interval for the difference, because it is the image of that interval under the reciprocal.

The omnibus test. Pearson's chi square test of equal responder proportions across the groups, without a continuity correction (chisq.test with correct = FALSE), on the number of groups minus 1 degrees of freedom. With two groups it tests \(\Delta = 0\). It and the Newcombe interval are different constructions and can disagree near the boundary of significance.

Edge cases.

  • Equal observed proportions: the difference is 0, the nnt row is Inf, its limits are NA, and the confidence set is two intervals.

  • No responder, or only responders, in one group: the Wilson limits stay inside [0, 1] and every row is reported. With none in one group and all in the other the difference is 1 or \(-1\) and the number needed to treat is 1.

  • No responder, or only responders, in every group: the proportions and their limits are reported, the difference is 0, and the chi square statistic is 0/0, so chi_square and p_value are NaN.

  • A group with one observation: its Wilson interval is reported (for one responder of one at the 95 percent level, 0.207 to 1), and so is everything built from it. The chi square approximation is poor with expected counts this small; no warning is given.

  • Outcomes equal to the threshold count as responders under both directions, so the counts under "ge" and "le" sum to more than the group size when there are such ties.

  • Missing values in x or group are removed before anything is counted. Fewer than two groups after that is an error, as are fewer than four values in x.

  • More than two groups: one row per group and the omnibus row. There is no difference or nnt row and no nnt_confidence_set attribute.

A worked example. In the first example below, 30 of 60 control participants and 35 of 60 treated participants gained at least 10 points. The responder proportions are 0.500 (95 percent Wilson interval 0.377 to 0.623) and 0.583 (0.457 to 0.699). The difference is 0.083, with the Newcombe interval \(-0.093\) to 0.252. The number needed to treat is 1/0.083 = 12. Because the interval for the difference includes zero, the nnt row has no limits; the confidence set is the two intervals whose finite ends are the reciprocals of the limits of the difference, \(1/(-0.093) = -10.8\) and \(1/0.252 = 3.97\): a number needed to treat of 3.97 or more in favor of treatment, or of 10.8 or more in favor of control. The chi square statistic is 0.839 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.360. The second example repeats the analysis at thresholds of 5 and 15: at 5 the difference is 0.183 (0.026 to 0.330), its interval excludes zero, and the number needed to treat is 5.45 with limits 3.03 and 37.98; at 15 the difference is 0.067 and its interval includes zero again. One trial thus gives three different answers at three thresholds, which is the reason to fix the threshold first and to show the sweep.

What the threshold costs. Dichotomizing an outcome discards information. For two variables that are bivariate normal, MacCallum, Zhang, Preacher, and Rucker (2002, pp. 24 to 26) show that splitting one of them at its mean multiplies their correlation by 0.798 and their squared correlation by 0.637, which for a test of zero correlation is about the same as discarding 36 percent of the sample, and that the loss grows as the split moves away from the mean. A responder threshold is such a split of the outcome. A responder analysis therefore complements, and never replaces, the analysis of the continuous outcome (Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027).

References

Altman, D. G. (1998). Confidence intervals for the number needed to treat. BMJ, 317(7168), 1309–1312. doi:10.1136/bmj.317.7168.1309

MacCallum, R. C., Zhang, S., Preacher, K. J., & Rucker, D. D. (2002). On the practice of dichotomization of quantitative variables. Psychological Methods, 7(1), 19–40. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.7.1.19

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

Newcombe, R. G. (1998). Interval estimation for the difference between independent proportions: Comparison of eleven methods. Statistics in Medicine, 17(8), 873–890. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19980430)17:8<873::AID-SIM779>3.0.CO;2-I

See also

ci_proportion for the per-group interval; nnt_from_smd for the model-based route to the number needed to treat from a standardized mean difference; cliff_delta and proportion_of_superiority for dominance-style effect sizes on the continuous outcome.

Other effect size estimates: cles(), cliff_delta(), correction_for_attenuation(), eta_squared(), eta_squared_generalized(), expected_partial_r(), expected_r(), expected_smd(), nnt_from_smd(), omega_squared(), probability_of_superiority_paired(), proportion_of_superiority(), smd_trimmed()

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# A two-arm trial: change scores, response defined as a gain of 10+.
# The interval for the difference includes zero, so the NNT row has no
# limits and the line under the table gives the two intervals.
set.seed(113)
change <- c(rnorm(60, 8, 9), rnorm(60, 13, 9))
arm    <- rep(c("control", "treatment"), each = 60)
res <- responder_analysis(change, arm, threshold = 10)
res
#>  group      n    responders estimate ci_lower ci_upper chi_square df   p_value
#>  control    60   30         0.500    0.377    0.623    <NA>       <NA> <NA>   
#>  treatment  60   35         0.583    0.457    0.699    <NA>       <NA> <NA>   
#>  difference <NA> <NA>       0.083    -0.093   0.252    <NA>       <NA> <NA>   
#>  nnt        <NA> <NA>       12.000   <NA>     <NA>     <NA>       <NA> <NA>   
#>  omnibus    <NA> <NA>       <NA>     <NA>     <NA>     0.839      1    0.3596 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> The interval for the difference includes 0, so the confidence set for the NNT, on the signed scale 1 / difference, is two intervals:
#> NNT <= -10.806 (control responds more often) or NNT >= 3.966 (treatment responds more often), joined at infinity (Altman, 1998)
attr(res, "nnt_confidence_set")
#>     lower     upper
#> 1    -Inf -10.80588
#> 2 3.96564       Inf

# How threshold-dependent is that conclusion?
responder_analysis(change, arm, threshold = 10, sweep = c(5, 15))
